posts.author: rustacean_ali
posts.title: After a year maintaining services in both Rust and Go, here's where each one actually hurt
posts.body:
We run eleven services: six in Go, five in Rust. People keep asking which is better, so here's the honest ledger.

Go hurt us in error handling verbosity and in the one service that genuinely needed predictable latency under GC pressure.

Rust hurt us in onboarding time (about six weeks before people were productive) and compile times in CI.

Neither hurt us where the internet says they would. Curious what others have seen.

comments.author: mira_k
comments.body: The onboarding number matches ours almost exactly. Weeks 3-5 are the wall; after that people stop fighting the borrow checker and start designing around ownership.

replies.author: first_job_fern
replies.body: As someone in week 4 right now: this is reassuring and terrifying in equal measure.

replies.author: rustacean_ali
replies.body: @first_job_fern the trick that helped our juniors: write it with `.clone()` everywhere first, then remove clones one at a time. You learn where ownership actually matters.

comments.author: dev_ostrander
comments.body: Did you measure the GC issue or just feel it? We saw something similar and it turned out to be an allocation-heavy JSON path, not the GC itself.

replies.author: rustacean_ali
replies.body: Measured — p99 spikes lined up with GC cycles in the traces. But you're right that reducing allocations got us 70% of the way before we rewrote anything.

comments.author: quant_priya
comments.body: Would love the CI numbers. Compile time is the thing I never see quantified in these comparisons.

posts.author: mira_k
posts.title: Keyset pagination cut our feed endpoint p95 from 480ms to 22ms
posts.body:
We were using OFFSET pagination on a table with ~40M rows. Page 200 meant Postgres scanning and discarding 4,000 rows every time.

Switching to a (rank, id) < (:rank, :id) predicate with a matching composite index made every page cost the same. The tricky part was the cursor: encode both values, never just the id.

comments.author: dev_ostrander
comments.body: The composite index ordering detail is the part everyone gets wrong. DESC on both columns or the planner won't use it for the row comparison.

comments.author: first_job_fern
comments.body: What do you do when the rank changes between page loads? Doesn't the user see duplicates?

replies.author: mira_k
replies.body: Occasionally, yes. We dedupe on the client by id. For a feed that's an acceptable trade; for anything financial it wouldn't be.

posts.author: first_job_fern
posts.title: How do you decide what deserves an integration test versus a unit test?
posts.body: My team's codebase has 1,900 unit tests and they all pass, and we still ship bugs at every boundary between services. Is there a rule of thumb people use?

comments.author: mira_k
comments.body: Mine: if the bug would come from two pieces of code disagreeing about something (a schema, a contract, a transaction boundary), it needs a test that runs both pieces for real.

comments.author: rustacean_ali
comments.body: Mock less. Most of the bugs I've shipped lived precisely in the thing I mocked.

posts.author: nadia_sec
posts.title: The beginner roadmap I wish someone had given me: networking first, tools last
posts.body:
Every week someone asks which certification to start with. My answer is always the same: none yet.

  1. Learn how a packet gets from your laptop to a server. DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP.
  2. Run a Linux box. Break it. Read its logs.
  3. Learn to read code in one language well enough to spot input handling.
  4. Only then pick tools and a cert.

People who skip step 1 can run tools but can't explain their output.

comments.author: first_job_fern
comments.body: How long did step 1 take you, realistically?

replies.author: nadia_sec
replies.body: Two or three months of evenings to be comfortable. You keep learning it forever, but that's the point where log files start making sense.

comments.author: dev_ostrander
comments.body: Strong agree on Linux. Half of incident response is knowing what normal looks like on a box.

comments.author: quant_priya
comments.body: Counterpoint: some people need the motivation of a cert milestone to keep going. I'd say do both in parallel, just don't treat the cert as the knowledge.

replies.author: nadia_sec
replies.body: Fair. Motivation is a real constraint. My concern is only people who stop at the cert.

posts.author: nadia_sec
posts.title: What we actually look for when hiring security interns
posts.body: Not certifications. We look for evidence of curiosity: a home lab write-up, a CTF solution explained clearly, a bug report to an open-source project. Writing matters more than people expect, because half the job is explaining risk to people who don't share your context.

comments.author: first_job_fern
comments.body: Does a blog with three posts count, or does it look worse than nothing?

replies.author: nadia_sec
replies.body: Three good posts beat thirty shallow ones. It counts.

posts.author: paperback_jo
posts.title: Non-fiction that reads like a novel: drop your best recommendations
posts.body: I'm in a fiction slump and want narrative non-fiction that actually pulls me forward. History, science, true events, anything. What kept you up past midnight?

comments.author: lena_lab
comments.body: Anything about the history of a scientific discovery told through the people involved. The personalities are half the story.

comments.author: tunde_builds
comments.body: Business histories of failed companies. The tension is built in because you know how it ends and still can't look away.

posts.author: first_job_fern
posts.title: Six months into my first job and I still feel slow. When did it click for you?
posts.body: Everyone on my team ships twice as fast as me. My manager says I'm on track but I don't feel it. Did anyone else feel like this, and when did it change?

comments.author: mira_k
comments.body: Around month nine for me. The thing that changed wasn't speed; it was that I started knowing which parts of the codebase I could ignore.

comments.author: quant_priya
comments.body: Your manager has information you don't: what 'on track' looks like across many new hires. Trust that signal more than your comparison with seniors.

comments.author: tunde_builds
comments.body: Write down one thing a week you couldn't do last month. Progress is invisible from the inside.

posts.author: quant_priya
posts.title: I've run 150 data science interviews. The candidates who stand out all do one thing
posts.body: They ask what decision the analysis is supposed to support before touching the data. It sounds trivial. Fewer than one in five candidates do it.

comments.author: lena_lab
comments.body: Academia trains the opposite instinct, which is probably why so many of us struggle in industry interviews.

posts.author: tunde_builds
posts.title: My first startup died with $200k still in the bank. Here's why stopping was the right call
posts.body:
We had 14 months of runway and a product nobody hated but nobody needed. Retention plateaued at 8% after week four for three straight quarters.

Returning money to investors was the hardest conversation I've had, and three of them backed my next company because of it.

comments.author: quant_priya
comments.body: What made you trust the 8% plateau instead of hoping the next feature would move it?

replies.author: tunde_builds
replies.body: We'd shipped six 'this will fix retention' features. The curve didn't move for any of them. At some point the data is telling you something about the problem, not the solution.

comments.author: dev_ostrander
comments.body: Respect for returning the money. Most people burn it to zero.

posts.author: lena_lab
posts.title: Why 'statistically significant' doesn't mean 'important': a short explainer
posts.body:
A p-value tells you how surprising your data would be if there were no effect. It says nothing about how big the effect is. With enough samples, a difference too small to matter will be 'significant'.

Always ask for the effect size and its confidence interval.

comments.author: quant_priya
comments.body: Saving this for the next time someone shows me a dashboard with 40 green p-values.

posts.author: coach_ines
posts.title: The boring program beats the perfect program you quit
posts.body: Three full-body sessions a week, a handful of compound lifts, add a little weight when it feels easy. That's it for the first year. Consistency is the variable that matters.

comments.author: dev_ostrander

posts.author: grid_and_type
posts.title: Pairing a serif for content with a sans for interface is still the best default
posts.body: Serif headlines signal 'read me'. A neutral sans for buttons and metadata signals 'operate me'. The split helps people know where they are on a dense page.

comments.author: mira_k
comments.body: Is this why documentation sites feel calmer than dashboards?

replies.author: grid_and_type
replies.body: Partly. Mostly it's that docs are allowed whitespace and dashboards are expected to justify every pixel.

posts.author: dev_ostrander
posts.title: What has AI-assisted coding actually changed on your team?
posts.body: Not predictions — observations. On ours: code review got longer, not shorter, and juniors ask fewer questions in public. I'm not sure the second one is good.

comments.author: mira_k
comments.body: Same review effect. The diffs are bigger and more plausible-looking, which is exactly what makes them slower to review.

comments.author: first_job_fern
comments.body: As a junior: I ask fewer questions because I'm afraid they're questions a tool could have answered. That's not great for learning.

replies.author: dev_ostrander
replies.body: That's the part that worries me. We started a 'no dumb questions' channel because of comments like this.

comments.author: rustacean_ali
comments.body: Boilerplate is cheaper. Design is not. Teams that confuse the two are going to have a rough few years.
